prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

National Health Interview Survey
 

About NHIS

For Everyone
June 18, 2026

What to know

  • NHIS is the National Health Interview Survey.
  • NHIS is a national survey that monitors the health of the U.S. population.
  • NHIS statistics provide insights into the health of people of different ages, sexes, races and ethnicities, geographic locations, and social and economic circumstances.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of people across the country—the U.S. population—by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics. NHIS focuses on the health of U.S. children and adults.

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) conducts NHIS. It is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey. NHIS began collecting data in 1957.

Each year, NHIS collects data from about 27,000 adults through confidential, face-to-face interviews throughout the year. Many of these adults also provide health information about children in their households.

NHIS collects data from civilians who don't live in institutions. Civilians are people not serving on active duty in the military. Institutionalized people live in places like correctional facilities, skilled-nursing homes, and mental (psychiatric) hospitals.

NCHS is exploring new ways for you to participate in NHIS. Some people may receive a paper questionnaire while others will receive an invitation to complete the survey online. Some people may receive both. Your participation matters no matter how you complete the survey. If you need assistance with the survey or have questions, please call the number on the letter you received or email nhis@census.gov.

Selected to participate in the survey?

Learn why you should take part in NHIS and what to expect.
Visit our participant website

What's collected

NHIS collects data through personal interviews. One adult household member provides information about their own health and the health of others in their households.

NHIS collects data about health topics like—

  • Illness and chronic conditions
  • Injuries and chronic pain
  • Health-related behaviors
  • Ability to perform daily activities (functioning) and disability
  • Healthcare access and use
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Preventive services to identify and prevent health problems

The U.S. Census Bureau employs and trains field staff to conduct these interviews. They follow procedures developed by NCHS experts. Field staff conduct most interviews in person. Sometimes they conduct follow-up interviews over the phone.

Did you know?

NHIS content is updated about every 15–20 years to reflect advances in survey methodology and coverage of health topics. In 2019, NHIS launched redesigned content and structure that differs from the earlier questionnaire design (1997–2018).

Data and documentation

NCHS publishes reports featuring expert analysis of NHIS data. Selected estimates also are available as part of our interactive data query systems that provide tables and charts.

In producing these resources, NHIS staff prioritize protecting participants' privacy.

Data files

NHIS public use data files are available to download in multiple formats. All potentially identifiable information has been removed to ensure the confidentiality of participants and their households.

NHIS restricted data files are available through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center (RDC) for a fee. To access restricted NHIS data, researchers must submit requests in the Standard Application Process portal. The RDC provides instructions for preparing and submitting an application to access restricted data.

NHIS data also has been linked with data from other sources. This provides more robust datasets that can be used to analyze complex relationships between data from different sources. These linked datasets are available in the RDC.

Find data documentation for these datasets at Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation.

How the data are used

NCHS staff use NHIS data to produce official national health estimates. One of NHIS's key strengths is its ability to produce estimates for many subgroups of the U.S. population. NHIS can do this because it collects data from such a large group of people.

NHIS health statistics provide health information by—

  • Demographic characteristics, like age and marital status
  • Geographic location, like region and metro area size
  • Social and economic circumstances, like employment status and poverty level

These data help researchers, policymakers, and other data users better understand how health differs among these groups.

NHIS data drive policies and programs to improve health. NHIS results have helped track the health status of Americans, their access to health care, and the nation's progress toward achieving health goals.

Contact us

Email nhis@cdc.gov with any questions about the National Health Interview Survey.

Related NHIS surveys

  • NHIS–Teen
  • 2014 Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 160 (Thursday, August 20, 2026)]
[Notices]
[Pages 53869-53871]
From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]
[FR Doc No: 2026-17040]



[[Page 53869]]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

[60Day-26-0214; Docket No. CDC-2026-1387]


Proposed Data Collection Submitted for Public Comment and 
Recommendations

AGENCY: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of 
Health and Human Services (HHS).

ACTION: Notice with comment period.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as part 
of its continuing effort to reduce public burden and maximize the 
utility of government information, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on a continuing 
information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 
1995. This notice invites comment on the National Health Interview 
Survey (NHIS). This Extension is designed to include the continuation 
of current questionnaire content and data collection operations in 
2027, as well as a systemic redesign of the NHIS to be implemented in 
2028.

DATES: Written comments must be received on or before October 19, 2026.

ADDRESSES: You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. CDC-2026-
1387 by either of the following methods:
     Federal eRulemaking Portal: www.regulations.gov. Follow 
the instructions for submitting comments.
     Mail: Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection Review 
Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road 
NE, MS H21-8, Atlanta, Georgia 30329.
    Instructions: All submissions received must include the agency name 
and Docket Number. CDC will post, without change, all relevant comments 
to www.regulations.gov.
    Please note: Submit all public comments through the Federal 
eRulemaking portal (www.regulations.gov) or by U.S. mail to the address 
listed above.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: To request more information on the 
proposed project or to obtain a copy of the information collection plan 
and instruments, contact Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection 
Review Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton 
Road NE, MS H21-8, Atlanta, Georgia 30329; Telephone: 404-639-7570; 
Email: [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 
(PRA) (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520), federal agencies must obtain approval from 
the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of 
information they conduct or sponsor. In addition, the PRA also requires 
federal agencies to provide a 60-day notice in the Federal Register 
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each new 
proposed collection, each proposed extension of existing collection of 
information, and each reinstatement of previously approved information 
collection before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To 
comply with this requirement, we are publishing this notice of a 
proposed data collection as described below.
    The OMB is particularly interested in comments that will help:
    1. Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is 
necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, 
including whether the information will have practical utility;
    2. Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of 
the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the 
methodology and assumptions used;
    3. Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to 
be collected;
    4. Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those 
who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, 
electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or 
other forms of information technology, e.g., permitting electronic 
submissions of responses; and
    5. Assess information collection costs.

Proposed Project

    National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) (OMB Control No. 0920-0214, 
Exp. 12/31/2026)--Revision--National Center for Health Statistics 
(NCHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Background and Brief Description

    Section 306 of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act (42 U.S.C.), as 
amended, authorizes that the Secretary of Health and Human Services 
(HHS), acting through NCHS, shall collect statistics on the extent and 
nature of illness and disability of the population of the United 
States. The annual National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is a major 
source of general statistics on the health of the U.S. population and 
has been in the field continuously since 1957. This voluntary and 
confidential household-based survey collects demographic and health-
related information from a nationally representative sample of 
households and noninstitutionalized, civilian persons throughout the 
country. NHIS data have long been used by government, academic, and 
private researchers to evaluate both general health and specific 
issues, such as smoking, diabetes, health care coverage, and access to 
health care. The survey is also a leading source of data for the 
Congressionally-mandated ``Health US'' and related publications, as 
well as the single most important source of statistics to track 
progress toward HHS health objectives.
    The current NHIS Sample Adult and Sample Child Questionnaires 
include annual core content that is scheduled to be fielded in the 
survey every year, rotating content that is fielded periodically, 
emerging content to address new topics of growing interest, and 
sponsored content that is fielded when external funding is available. 
Rotating Sample Adult and Sample Child core content on service 
utilization, physical activity (including walking for adults), and 
sleep that was on the NHIS in 2026 will rotate off in 2027. Content on 
alcohol use, fatigue, and smoking history and cessation will also 
rotate off the sample Adult Core, and content on height and weight, 
neighborhood characteristics, and screen time will rotate off the 
Sample Child core. The 2027 Sample Adult rotating core will include 
items on chronic conditions, allergies, and hearing and communication--
content previously fielded on the 2024 NHIS. It will also include 
content on preventative screening and aspirin use, and chronic pain, 
content that was previously fielded in 2025. Content on injuries and 
detailed employment information that was fielded on the 2026 Sample 
Adult survey will continue in 2027. The 2027 Sample Child content will 
include questions on injuries (continuing from 2026), allergies 
(previously fielded in 2024) and stressful life events (previously 
fielded in 2025).
    Sponsored content on complementary and integrative health, using 
questions similar to those previously fielded in 2022, will be included 
on both the 2027 Sample Adult and Sample Child Questionnaires. Sample 
Adult and Child Questionnaires for 2027 will also include vision and 
other difficulties with taste, smell, hearing and communication using 
similar questions to those fielded in 2023.
    Sponsored content from the 2026 Adult and Child Questionnaires on

[[Page 53870]]

chronic fatigue will remain in 2027. Sponsored content from the 2026 
Adult Questionnaire on life satisfaction, diabetes, social support, 
loneliness, and isolation, tobacco product use, chronic fatigue, 
immunizations, whole person health, and social functioning and age of 
disability onset will also remain. Sponsored content on the 2027 Adult 
Questionnaire will also include questions on cancer screening, 
caregiving, epilepsy, and psoriasis, similar to questions previously 
fielded in 2025, and questions on occupational health, psoriasis and 
Crohn's/ulcerative colitis, similar to questions fielded in 2023 and 
2024.
    Like in past years, and in accordance with the 1995 initiative to 
increase the integration of surveys within the HHS, respondents to the 
2027 NHIS will serve as the sampling frame for the Medical Expenditure 
Panel Survey conducted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and 
Quality (AHRQ). A subsample of NHIS respondents and/or members of 
commercial survey panels may be identified to participate in short 
methodological and cognitive testing activities to evaluate the 
questionnaire and/or inform work to redesign the data collection 
methods and questionnaires for 2028. In addition, subsamples of NHIS 
respondents may be recontacted by web, phone, or mail to ask follow-up 
questions on topics that are already included in the NHIS. The NHIS 
also includes content that is used to benchmark estimates and calibrate 
survey weights from probability-based online commercial survey panels 
as part of the NCHS Rapid Surveys System.
    To maintain data quality and contain operational costs, a redesign 
of the NHIS is being planned for implementation in 2028. The redesigned 
NHIS will expand upon the strengths of the current in-person data 
collection methodology by incorporating lower-cost, self-administered 
data collection modes to account for respondent preferences and reduce 
operational costs. This will be done using a sequential mixed-mode data 
collection approach in which sampled households are first invited to 
respond using self-administered online and paper questionnaires. Census 
Bureau field representatives will then conduct in-person follow-up for 
some households that do not respond to self-response modes, preserving 
the long-standing quality standards of the NHIS while modernizing its 
operational model. This mixed-mode design will be refined through a 
series of cognitive, usability, and field tests. This redesign of both 
survey operations and questionnaire content is strategically timed to 
coordinate with the data cycle used to monitor Healthy People 2030 
objectives, providing a timely transition into the next decade of 
monitoring the nation's critical public health indicators. It is also 
timed to coincide with the Census Bureau's deployment of its new 
modernized data collection program--Data Ingest and Collection for the 
Enterprise (DICE)--that will improve the NHIS's ability to collect data 
from respondents through paper, internet, and interviewer-assisted 
modes.
    The redesigned 2028 NHIS will continue to include an Adult 
Questionnaire completed by one randomly selected adult aged 18 or older 
in each sampled household. Consistent with current practices, 
information about the selected adult will be collected from the adult 
himself/herself unless s/he is physically or mentally unable to do so, 
in which case a knowledgeable proxy will be allowed to answer for the 
adult. The redesigned 2028 NHIS will also continue to include questions 
regarding one randomly selected child under age 18 in each household 
with children. Information about the child will be collected from a 
parent or guardian living with the child. Draft questionnaires for both 
adults and children have been included in this docket for public review 
and comment. The draft 2028 questionnaires can also be viewed on the 
NHIS website at https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/2028-questionnaire-redesign.html. It is expected that these questionnaires will be revised 
following the public comment period.
    The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is particularly 
interested in comments that support the planning of the redesign to be 
implemented in 2028. Comments are especially welcome regarding the 
structure, length, and clarity of the redesigned adult and child 
questionnaires; the implications of adopting a sequential mixed-mode 
design; the importance of specific content additions or removals; and 
the potential effect of these changes on data quality, usability, and 
trend measurement. Commenters who suggest questionnaire additions are 
encouraged to identify the minimum question sets to meet identified 
data needs. NCHS is also interested in comments on the practical 
utility of child-level data collection that is largely limited to 
domains for which all-person population estimates are desired (i.e., 
population estimates that have historically relied on data from both 
the adult and child-focused interviews).
    The redesigned questionnaires will retain key health measures that 
are essential for tracking public health trends. Key health measures in 
the draft adult questionnaire include longstanding items on major 
chronic health conditions, foundational measures of disability and 
functional status based on the Washington Group Short Set, and key 
measures of health insurance coverage, continuity, and adequacy. Topic 
areas in this draft questionnaire also include healthcare utilization, 
access to care, medication use, and prescription nonadherence. 
Behavioral and demographic covariates are also included. The draft 
adult questionnaire introduces several new content areas to reflect 
contemporary health information needs. These include a recently 
validated summary measure of overall health and well-being known as the 
Whole Person Health Index and new questions on high-deductible health 
plans, insurance adequacy, primary care, asthma treatment, and 
marijuana use.
    Because the redesigned NHIS will include self-administered online 
and mailed questionnaires, the redesigned 2028 questionnaire will 
necessarily be shorter in length and less complicated in structure, as 
compared to the current questionnaire. Many of the more detailed 
questions on particular topics that were fielded annually from 2019 to 
2027 are not included in the draft adult questionnaire for 2028. Also, 
the redesigned NHIS questionnaire structure does not include a detailed 
schedule of content that rotates on and off the survey with a set 
periodicity established years in advance. This change is necessary to 
both shorten the questionnaire and to preserve an agile and dynamic 
design that allows for the addition of content on topics of current and 
emerging interest. Space will still be reserved for federal agencies to 
fund sponsored content. For example, in 2028, NCHS anticipates 
including sponsored content on screening for breast, cervical, and 
colorectal cancer and on injury, among others.
    OMB Clearance is sought for three years, to collect data for 2027-
2029. For 2027 data collection, the docket includes detailed 
descriptions of sampling, questionnaires, data collection procedures, 
and other survey design components. These details have not yet been 
finalized for the 2028 and 2029 data collections. Therefore, the plans 
for the updated survey design are described only at a high level in 
this package. NCHS will submit more details regarding 2028 data 
collection, including revised questionnaires, to the Office of 
Management and Budget for approval in 2027.

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Health Interview Survey (NHIS): Dataset Report

**Research date:** early October 2026. I took most of this from primary sources: CDC/NCHS pages, OMB clearance documents, the Federal Register, and the 2025 NHIS documentation. Some details come from my general background knowledge, and I've marked those where they matter.

---

## 1. Checking your description

Your description is accurate. It closely follows CDC's own "About NHIS" page (last updated June 18, 2026), which says NHIS "is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey… began collecting data in 1957… collects data from about 27,000 adults through confidential, face-to-face interviews." A few points need context:

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Publisher: CDC / NCHS** | Correct. NCHS designs the survey, sponsors it, processes the data and publishes it. The **U.S. Census Bureau** hires and trains the field interviewers and collects the data under NCHS procedures. The President's FY2026 and FY2027 budget requests also propose **moving NCHS out of CDC** into a new HHS "Office of Strategy." If that happens, the listed publisher may change. |
| **"Since 1957"** | Correct. Data collection started in July 1957 and has run every year since. |
| **"About 27,000 adults each year"** | Roughly right, but recent numbers are lower. The **2025** file has **24,215 sample adults and 6,049 sample children in 25,182 households**. Before 2019 the survey covered about 35,000 households and roughly 87,500 people a year, with a different file structure. |
| **"Face-to-face interviews"** | Only partly true now. In-person interviewing is the official default, but in 2025 **53.1% of sample-adult and 54.3% of sample-child interviews were done at least partly by telephone**. From **2028**, NHIS plans to become a web, mail and in-person survey (see §4). CDC's page already says some people may get paper or online questionnaires. |
| **"Largest" national health survey** | This is NCHS's own description. CDC's BRFSS interviews more people each year, but it is a state-based telephone survey. "Largest and oldest *household interview* health survey" is the more defensible wording. |
| **"Confidential"** | Correct. The survey is voluntary and confidential under federal law (see §2). |

## 2. Legal authority and mandate

- **Founding law:** The National Health Survey Act of 1956 (Public Law 84‑652), signed by President Eisenhower on July 3, 1956. It created a continuing national health survey program and explicitly authorized research on survey methods and cooperation with other agencies.
- **Current authority:** Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 242k). It directs the HHS Secretary, acting through NCHS, to "collect statistics on the extent and nature of illness and disability of the population of the United States" (as quoted in the 2026 Federal Register notice).
- **Confidentiality:** Section 308(d) of the PHS Act (42 U.S.C. 242m(d)) and the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA, reauthorized in 2018 as Title III of the Evidence Act). Identifiable data may be used only for statistical purposes.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB Control No. **0920‑0214**, which expires 12/31/2026. NCHS has asked for a three-year renewal covering 2027–2029 (Federal Register, Aug. 20, 2026, Docket **CDC‑2026‑1387**). **Public comments are due October 19, 2026**, so policy advocates should note the deadline.
- **Statutory reporting role:** NHIS is a main source for the congressionally mandated *Health, United States* report. The Federal Register notice calls it "the single most important source of statistics to track progress toward HHS health objectives," including Healthy People 2030.

## 3. History

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1956 | National Health Survey Act passed |
| July 1957 | NHIS fieldwork begins, with the Census Bureau collecting the data |
| 1960 | NCHS is formed and becomes the survey's home (from my background knowledge) |
| 1982 | Questionnaire split into a basic core plus rotating topical modules |
| After each census (1985, 1995, 2006, 2016) | Sample redesigned. The 1985 redesign enabled linkage to administrative records and let NHIS serve as a sampling frame for other surveys. |
| 1997 | Major redesign into Household, Family, Sample Adult and Sample Child components; CAPI (laptop) interviewing |
| 2010–2015 | Sample increased after the Affordable Care Act to support state-level insurance estimates |
| 2013 | Sexual orientation questions added |
| 2014 | Separate Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS |
| 2016 | New sample design based on commercial address lists, planned for 2016–2025 (could run to 2027). About 35,000 target households, with a stable core of 25,000; extra sample for the smallest states and DC. |
| 2019 | Questionnaire redesign. The Family file was dropped and the survey moved to annual core, rotating core (3-year cycle), emerging and sponsored content. This creates a **trend break with 1997–2018**. |
| 2020–2021 | COVID-19 forced telephone-heavy interviewing; NHIS became a key source for Long COVID estimates |
| 2022 | Gender identity questions added on an experimental basis |
| 2025 | Gender identity questions **removed** to comply with Executive Order 14168 (change request filed March 20, 2025; sexual orientation questions kept). Fieldwork **paused Oct 1–Nov 17, 2025** during the funding lapse. About 110 NCHS staff got layoff notices in October 2025, nearly a quarter of the workforce; all were rescinded by Nov 18. |
| Sept 30, 2026 | 2025 public-use files released |
| 2026 | NHIS-Teen not run; new sponsored content added (GLP‑1 drugs, nicotine pouches, social functioning, hearing, and more) |
| 2028 (planned) | Major redesign: sequential mixed-mode design and a **much shorter questionnaire** |

## 4. The planned 2028 redesign

This is the biggest upcoming change for anyone tracking the series.

- Households will first be invited to answer **online or on paper**. Census field representatives will follow up in person with some non-responders. The redesign is timed to match the Census Bureau's new "DICE" data collection platform and the Healthy People 2030 data cycle.
- NCHS's question-evaluation plan says the questionnaire will be "shortened significantly" with "substantial cuts" to content. Priority goes to topics NCHS is legally required to cover and to key HHS indicators.
- The fixed rotating-content schedule ends.
- The survey keeps:
  - chronic conditions
  - the Washington Group disability questions
  - health insurance coverage, continuity and adequacy
  - use of and access to care
  - medications and skipped prescriptions
- New content: a Whole Person Health Index, high-deductible health plans, primary care, asthma treatment and marijuana use.
- Planned annual numbers for 2028–2029: about 65,000 household rosters, 40,000 adult questionnaires and 10,000 child questionnaires, plus a small adolescent follow-up survey.
- NCHS is asking for comments on how the redesign will affect **trend measurement**, and on whether child-level data are still worth collecting.

**Implication:** Expect possible mode effects and a new series break in 2028. Many detailed 2019–2027 items will probably end.

## 5. Design and methodology (for data scientists)

- **Population covered:** The civilian, non-institutionalized population of the 50 states and DC. It excludes active-duty military, civilians living on military bases, people in nursing homes and prisons, and people with no fixed address.
- **Sample design:** A stratified cluster sample drawn mainly from commercial address lists, with field listing in some areas. Each quarter's sample is nationally representative.
- **Who answers:**
  - A household roster covering everyone.
  - One randomly selected adult, who answers for themselves unless unable to.
  - One randomly selected child, reported by a knowledgeable adult.
- **Analysis variables (2019 onward):** weights `WTFA_A` (adults) and `WTFA_C` (children); stratum `PSTRAT`; PSU `PPSU`. Use Taylor-series linearization for variance. Use survey-aware software such as R `survey`, SAS `SURVEY` procedures or Stata `svy`.
- **Response rates:** Falling over time. 2025 weighted AAPOR RR2 was **41.3% for adults and 42.0% for children**.
- **Respondent burden:** About 48–56 minutes for the adult questionnaire; total annual burden around 37,500–39,000 hours.
- **Quality control:** Fewer than 5% of households are re-interviewed. Paradata files and imputed income files are released.
- **Geography:** National, census region, and metro status within region. NHIS is not designed to give precise annual estimates for every state; state and sub-state identifiers are restricted.
- **Comparability warnings:**
  - There are breaks at 1982, 1997 and 2019, with 2028 coming.
  - Collection modes in 2020–2021 and 2025 were unusual.
  - Content rotates, so many topics appear only every two or three years.

---

## 6. Access, formats and products

- **Public-use files:** Free to download on the NHIS documentation pages for each year and on `ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/`.
  - Recent years come in CSV and SAS formats.
  - Older years are fixed-width ASCII with SAS, SPSS or Stata input programs.
  - Each year includes questionnaires, codebooks, survey descriptions and a PRICSSA reporting checklist.
- **Restricted files:** Available through the NCHS Research Data Center for a fee. Applications go through the Standard Application Process portal at researchdatagov.org. Restricted items include geography, detailed dates and unmasked variables.
- **Linked data:**
  - National Death Index mortality linkage: restricted files cover NHIS 1986–2021, with follow-up through Dec 31, 2022. Public-use linked mortality files (with some values perturbed) cover 1986–2018.
  - CMS Medicare and Medicaid (T-MSIS), Social Security Administration, HUD housing assistance and the U.S. Renal Data System. These are mostly restricted.
  - Public-use synthetic linked files and Medicare feasibility files.
- **Ready-made estimates:**
  - Early Release Program (quarterly health insurance estimates and key indicators)
  - Interactive Summary Health Statistics
  - the NCHS Data Query System
  - *Health, United States*
  - NCHS Data Briefs, National Health Statistics Reports and the *Vital and Health Statistics* Series 2 and 10
  - Wireless Substitution reports on cell-phone-only households, which pollsters use widely
- **Third-party copies:** **IPUMS NHIS** at the University of Minnesota provides harmonized, free microdata that, to my knowledge, go back to the 1960s; it is the easiest way to analyze long trends. **ICPSR** also holds historical NHIS files.
- **Contacts:** nhis@cdc.gov; the NHIS listserv for release news; nhis@census.gov for survey participants.
- **Terms of use:** Federal government work. Public-use files come with NCHS data-use restrictions that prohibit any attempt to identify respondents, under PHS Act §308(d).

---

## 7. Who uses it

- **Federal agencies:**
  - HHS uses it for Healthy People and *Health, United States*.
  - AHRQ draws the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) sample from NHIS respondents, under a 1995 HHS survey-integration initiative.
  - CDC programs on tobacco, diabetes, cancer screening, immunization and disability rely on it.
  - NIH institutes and others pay for sponsored questions.
  - NCHS uses NHIS to benchmark and calibrate the weights of its online Rapid Surveys System panels.
- **Policy analysts** such as CBO, ASPE, KFF, Urban Institute, SHADAC and the Commonwealth Fund use it to track insurance coverage, including ACA effects and the uninsured rate.
- **Academic researchers** in epidemiology, health economics, demography, disability studies and disparities research. Linked mortality files make it possible to study long-term outcomes.
- **Journalists, advocates and pollsters**, including users of the wireless substitution estimates.

---

## 8. Public benefits

- It is the longest-running continuous national record of Americans' health, spanning nearly 70 years.
- It provides official national estimates of chronic disease, disability, insurance and access to care, with enough sample to break results down by race and ethnicity, income, age and region.
- It is the evidence base for major policy: insurance reform, tobacco control, vaccination, disability policy and Long COVID.
- It supports other national data systems: the MEPS sampling frame, panel calibration and linked administrative research files.
- Its microdata and documentation are free and well documented, which allows independent checking of government claims.

---

## 9. Risks and issues for preservationists and advocates

1. **Content cuts:** The 2028 shortening will drop many detailed items. The questions removed in 2025 (gender identity) break the series for LGBTQ+ health research. The Williams Institute and KFF have documented these removals.
2. **Funding and capacity:**
   - NCHS's budget was flat at $187.4M in FY2025.
   - The FY2026 request was $175M; the American Statistical Association estimates NCHS has lost about 24% of its purchasing power since FY2009.
   - NCHS lost about 10% of its staff in 2025, plus the October 2025 layoff notices.
   - NHIS depends on funding from other agencies for its core operations.
3. **Governance:** The proposed move to an HHS Office of Strategy, alongside ASPE and AHRQ, raises questions about the agency's independence and continuity.
4. **Website instability:** CDC pages were reorganized in 2024–2025, and an AJPH article reports attempts to remove archived data, variables and documentation, which lawsuits pushed back. Old `.htm` addresses have changed. **Archive the documentation along with the data.** That means questionnaires, codebooks, variance and weighting guidance, and the "Survey Description" PDFs for each year.
5. **Falling response rates** (now about 41%) and changing collection modes threaten comparability over time.
6. **Preservation checklist:**
   - Mirror the FTP directories for data and documentation for all years.
   - Mirror the linked-file documentation.
   - Save the Early Release and Data Query System outputs.
   - Save the OMB clearance packages (on omb.report and reginfo.gov), which record question changes year by year.
   - Save the Federal Register notices.
   - Capture the 2028 draft questionnaires from the regulations.gov docket.
   - Treat IPUMS and ICPSR copies as backups held outside the government.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

# NHIS Risk Assessment

**Assessed:** October 8, 2026. Most of the evidence below comes from primary sources: CDC/NCHS pages, the Federal Register, OMB filings and NHIS documentation. Items from my own background knowledge are marked.

**Overall:** Old data looks safe. The main risks are to future data: the survey is shrinking, NCHS (the National Center for Health Statistics, which runs it) is weaker, and a presidential order has already changed what it collects. Policy and Data Quality rate **High**. Future Data Availability and Staffing and Funding rate **Moderate**. Historical Data Availability and Statutory Context show **No Known Issue**.

**About the staffing tracker:** The USAJobs tracker you suggested stopped collecting data on December 31, 2025, and it counts job postings, not staff. I used staffing figures from the American Statistical Association (ASA), the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), the CDC workers' union and Michigan State University instead.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for Moderate:**
- In January 2025, after the "gender ideology" executive order, datasets and documents about sexual orientation and gender identity were pulled from CDC websites. A court order temporarily blocked this (Williams Institute). I found no evidence that NHIS files were among those changed.
- NHIS asked gender identity questions experimentally in 2022–2024 (the 2023 survey description lists the topic). Because the questions were later removed (see Policy), those older variables may face future pressure.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The 2019–2025 data, questionnaires and documentation are all on the NHIS documentation pages. Files for 1997–2018 and 1996-and-earlier are in the CDC Archive.
- Full documentation and file checksums for 2024 are still on ftp.cdc.gov.
- Restricted variable lists going back to 1997 are still published.
- Full copies exist outside the government at IPUMS and ICPSR.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** I found no record of NHIS files or variables being removed. The move of pre-2019 material to the CDC Archive is a relocation, not a removal. It's still worth mirroring that archive.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for High:**
- Fieldwork stopped from October 1 to November 17, 2025, during the government shutdown, so about seven weeks of collection were lost.
- The teen survey (NHIS-Teen) did not run in 2026.
- Even so, the 2025 annual files were released, and the survey's OMB approval has not lapsed.

**Evidence for Moderate:**
- **The 2025 public-use files came out late, on September 30, 2026** (NCHS blog). The 2024 files came out June 24, 2025, so this was about three months behind the usual schedule.
- OMB approval (control no. 0920-0214) expires **December 31, 2026**. The 60-day comment notice only appeared on August 20, 2026 (91 FR 53869). A 30-day notice and OMB review still have to happen before year-end.
- The comment deadline is October 19 in the Federal Register but October 20 on the CDC redesign page.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The 2025 early-release estimates came out on time, on May 28, 2026.
- OMB approval is still active, and the renewal request covers 2027–2029.

**Rating: Moderate.** The annual release slipped and collection was partly interrupted, but the survey continues and its approval is still valid.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for High:**
- **Sample sizes fell sharply:**

  | | 2024 | 2025 | Change |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Sample adults | 32,629 | 24,215 | about −26% |
  | Sample children | 8,360 | 6,049 | about −28% |
  | Households | 33,917 | 25,182 | |

- **Response rates fell:** adults from 47.9% to 41.3%, children from 45.8% to 42.0%.
- The annual release was about three months later than usual (less timely).
- Gender identity questions were removed in 2025, so that breakdown no longer exists.
- NHIS-Teen was skipped in 2026 (less frequent).

**Evidence for Moderate (future risk):**
- The 2028 redesign (Federal Register docket CDC-2026-1387) switches to web and paper first. NCHS's own planning document says the questionnaire will be "shortened significantly," with "substantial cuts."
- NCHS is openly asking whether collecting data on children is still useful.
- NCHS itself asks for comment on how the changes will affect trend measurement, which signals a likely break in the time series.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The core content and quarterly early-release program continue.
- New sponsored topics were added in 2026.

**Rating: High.** Fewer interviews, a later release, removed questions and a skipped teen survey are reductions that have already happened. The 2028 changes add more risk.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for High or Moderate:** None found. No other survey could replace NHIS. The state-based telephone survey BRFSS uses different methods, and the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) draws its sample *from* NHIS.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The National Health Survey Act of 1956 (P.L. 84-652) created the survey.
- Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 242k) explicitly directs NCHS to collect statistics on "the extent and nature of illness and disability."
- It supports federal programs:
  - It is the sampling frame for the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's MEPS.
  - It is the main data source for Healthy People 2030 and the congressionally mandated report *Health, United States*.
  - It is used to calibrate NCHS's Rapid Surveys System.
- The FY2027 budget request itself funds NCHS to "maintain core data systems."

**Rating: No Known Issue.**

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High:**
- CDC as a whole lost about 30% of its staff (around 3,810 people) between March 2025 and May 2026, according to a union-backed analysis. OPM data show CDC falling from 12,934 to 9,453 employees.
- CDC Director Susan Monarez was fired in August 2025 (my background knowledge).
- In October 2025, about 110 NCHS staff received layoff notices, nearly 25% of its workforce (AJPH). All were rescinded by November 18, 2025.

**Evidence for Moderate:**
- **NCHS lost roughly 14–20% of its staff.** ASA's 2026 midyear update shows about 451 → 368. Its Fall 2025 estimate was about 10%.
- Contract terminations weakened report publication and data release (ASA).
- **Leadership:** Director Brian Moyer retired, and Carolyn Greene has been acting director since. CDC's leadership page lists the NCHS director post as "Vacant," and a job posting closed July 30, 2026.
- The FY2026 and FY2027 budget requests both propose moving NCHS out of CDC into a new HHS Office of Strategy.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The FY2026 appropriation held NCHS flat at **$187.4M**; Congress rejected the proposed cut of about 7%.
- The FY2027 request is $175M, a 6.6% cut, which is below the 10% threshold.
- ASA estimates NCHS has lost about 19–24% of its purchasing power since FY2009.

**Rating: Moderate.** At the NCHS level, the publishing unit, staff losses fall in the 10–39% range, the director post is filled on an acting basis, and a reorganization is pending. If you judge at the CDC level instead, it would be High.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for High:**
- **An OMB change request driven by a presidential action:** in March 2025, NCHS removed the gender identity question and its write-in follow-up, citing **Executive Order 14168**. NCHS confirmed this to NPR, and KFF and the Williams Institute document it.
- The change was made through a "non-substantive" request, with no public notice-and-comment.

**Evidence for Moderate:**
- The proposed move to the HHS Office of Strategy (FY2026 and FY2027 budgets).
- The planned 2028 content cuts, and NCHS's open question about dropping detailed child data.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Sexual orientation questions were kept.
- I found no negative policy note on the NHIS site.

**Rating: High.** A collection change explicitly driven by an executive order meets the rubric's definition.
